The operations studies were on a monthly basis for the period 1900 through 1973 and used flow data adjusted to current Rio Grande basin development. Major Rio Grande floods which occurred during this 1900-1973 period were also studies using a 6-hour computational interval. These floods were routed through Amistad and Falcon Reservoirs with starting reservoir elevations established by the monthly operations studies. The IBWC flood routings have been considered as a part of the various operations studies and information regarding reservoir pool levels and outflows considers both the monthly studies and the more detailed flood routings. All studies used the latest court adjudicated criteria for meeting irrigation and domestic requirements as developed by the Texas Water Rights Commission and the rules of allocation for release of United States water from Amistad and Falcon Reservoirs.
4.17 Included among the various operations studies were Study A for future conditions without the addition of hydroelectric generating facilities at Amistad Dam and Study B for future conditions with the proposed action of adding hydroelectric facilities to the United States side of Amistad Dam. The probable impact of the proposed action on the hydrologic aspects of the environment are presented graphically in a comparison between the results of Study A and Study B, on plates IV-1, IV-2, IV-3.
4.18 Falcon Reservoir. There will be no change in the rules which govern releases of flood or irrigation and domestic waters from Falcon Reservoir. Studies by the US Section, IBWC indicate that monthly Rio Grande flows below Falcon and monthly in flows into the Gulf of Mexico will not be affected by the proposed action (see plate IV-3). In summary, those water users downstream from Falcon will continue to be served in the future as they have been in the past.
4.19 To optimize electrical energy from the two lake system, there will be additional releases from Amistad Reservoir. The net effect of these hydroelectric releases from Amistad will slightly raise the conservation pool at Falcon Reservoir.
4.20 Amistad Reservoir. The primary difference in the operation of Amistad Reservoir as a result of the proposed action is that normal releases (irrigation and municipal) will be made through the turbines instead of over the spillway. To optimize electrical energy from the two lake system, there will be additional water releases from Amistad Reservoir. These additional releases will be reregulated at Falcon Reservoir. No releases from Amistad for hydroelectric power production will directly result in flood spills at Falcon Reservoir or in the transfer of ownership of water.
4.21 There will be no change in the release of flood waters from Amistad, except that a part of flood flow will pass through the powerhouse to generate electricity. When it is necessary to release more flood waters than can be used for power, flood gates will be used.
4.22 The schedule of hydropower releases from Amistad powerplant cannot be specifically forecast because they will naturally vary from day to day depending on changing energy demands. However, very generally, the daily release pattern is likely to vary from 4 to 14 hours in length at a rate of 4,000 cfs. This 4,000 cfs release would slightly drawdown Amistad Reservoir.
